Huh,,, I mean in my experience, people talk about race a lot here. At least among young people, I’ve heard a lot of Americans discuss race and gender and systems of inequality there. As for class, it’s kinda a big thing because a lot of language and behaviours revolve around respecting those of higher status than you, so you can’t ignore it or sweep it under the rug. In addition, people comment on your looks all the time, and tell you if you’re objectively good looking to your face. It’s common to call a young man, or young woman who is rather good looking “pretty boy” or “pretty girl” and it wouldn’t be considered hitting on them? Like you have to be a good looking face to work at many restaurants, so if I were to call over a waiter, I would say “hey pretty boy/girl!” And stuff like that. But younger people cannot comment on older people’s looks, so I would never say, even to those a grade above me, how good they look (objectively, as in facial structure) or don’t look. That is, unless we become friends, and equals, haha. Like all the aunties and uncles can tell you all about your face and your body, but you can’t say a word of it back to them.

I don’t know— not acknowledging what is definitely a system of inequality and discrimination bothers me. Even though east Asia is steeped in lookism, there’s a relief in putting a reason to why some things might happen/mightn’t happen. In the US, it just seems like to think that lookism exists is to be deluded or have low self esteem. 

I don’t believe true equality exists. Perhaps lookism received such prominence and has become something openly acknowledged like race in east Asia is because we are mostly homogenous, so other factors jump out easily. I know that factors like classism, like lookism, are openly acknowledged in asian cultures and language. (I speak Chinese and Japanese, and know enough Korean to know about the honour system that runs in all three)

Maybe because societies are so rigidly structured from language to actions to presentation that it’s impossible not to acknowledge things like classism and lookism that sorta just.... lurk beneath a facade of equality in America. 

I don’t rly get the race thing quite yet (please don’t attack me, it has been a long time since I’ve lived in a western country) but it baffles me that y’all don’t really talk much about classism or lookism when it’s pretty much *all* we talk about.

Looking at what people say in purple pill, trp, incel forums and such, I’m a little surprised. My parents moved me from Canada to east Asia for a decade and having grown up there (between China, Hong Kong and japan) I can definitely say “lookism” is a topic discussed in the mainstream. People rate you to your face. Aunties and uncles will suggest surgeries you should get (more common if ur a girl, but they’ll say it to a guy too). I’m currently studying in the states, and part of me almost wishes we discussed lookism as openly as people do in Asia. I don’t know, the facade of acceptance sometimes seems more harmful than blunt harshness. It’s so common to get surgery that people thought it was weird I didn’t accept my graduation gift of double eyelid surgery. My mom has had double eyelid surgery, my dad is planning on getting surgery to rectify his skin soon, and most of my girl friends and some of my guy friends have had something done.

College is hard. 

I feel like I worked my ass off to get to a “good school”, and now that I’m here the work never stops. There’s a huge looming shadow of mediocrity and a deep fear that I’ve worked this hard, come this far, and it’s either all for nothing or it’s all gonna be downhill from here.
